title: Australia’s critical-minerals strategy has a Brazil-sized gap
gist: A Brazilian economist argues Australia's new A$1.2 billion Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve names Canada, Europe, Japan, South Korea, the UK and the US as partners but omits Brazil — despite Brazil holding the world's second-largest rare-earth reserves and dominating niobium production — and proposes a concrete bilateral compact (paired rare-earth separation and processing pilot projects) so both countries stop being mere price-taking ore exporters to industrial buyers who hold the real processing leverage.

themes.theme: The gap: Brazil is missing from Australia's reserve

insights.claim: Australia's new Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve commits A$1.2 billion to secure antimony, gallium and rare earths and is explicitly designed to work with international partners named as Canada, Europe, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States — Brazil is not named despite ongoing bilateral contact, including a February meeting between Australia's ambassador in Brasília and Brazil's National Mining Agency.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named gap (Brazil's absence from a A$1.2bn strategic minerals reserve) that could be closed — relevant to tracking whether Australia's critical minerals partner list expands to include Brazil in future policy updates.
insights.locator: From São Paulo, Australia's new Critical Minerals

insights.claim: Brazil has the world's second-largest rare-earth reserves, dominates global niobium production, and holds major deposits of lithium, graphite, nickel and copper; Austrade expects Brazil's mining sector to attract almost US$77 billion in investment between 2026 and 2030.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Quantifies Brazil's scale as a critical-minerals resource base (2nd-largest rare-earth reserves, niobium dominance, US$77bn projected 2026-2030 investment) — a major emerging-market minerals opportunity currently underweighted in Australia's strategic partnerships.

themes.theme: Shared structural weakness: extraction without pricing power

insights.claim: Australia and Brazil face the same uncomfortable problem: both can extract minerals at scale, while much of the processing expertise, industrial demand and pricing power sits elsewhere, meaning both currently function mainly as suppliers of raw material to more powerful downstream industrial buyers.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Core investment thesis: raw extraction capacity alone does not confer pricing power in critical minerals; the value (and margin) sits in processing/refining, which both Australia and Brazil currently lack relative to their extraction scale.
insights.quote: Australia and Brazil face the same uncomfortable problem: both can extract minerals at scale, while much of the processing expertise, industrial demand and pricing power sits elsewhere.
insights.locator: For now, Canberra mostly treats Brazil

insights.claim: Australia and Brazil together account for roughly a third of global iron ore exports and are competing for the same pool of capital to fund new mineral-chain projects, but competing only on the price of ore, tax concessions or approval speed will leave both as price takers, with industrial buyers retaining leverage.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Quantifies the two countries' combined global iron ore market share (~33%) while warning that framing them as competitors rather than potential collaborators on processing leaves both structurally disadvantaged versus industrial buyers.
insights.locator: The two countries are usually described as competitors

insights.claim: The author proposes Canberra and Brasília select one rare-earth separation project in Brazil and one processing or materials-qualification project in Australia, each with an identified industrial customer, a solvable technical bottleneck, and a pilot-production timetable — arguing this would be more useful than another broad memorandum of understanding.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable bilateral project template (paired pilot projects with named industrial customers) rather than another diplomatic MOU — worth tracking whether Australian or Brazilian agencies announce such paired pilot projects.
insights.locator: A bilateral compact should therefore begin small

insights.claim: Australia's ANSTO and CSIRO could work with Brazil's Centre for Mineral Technology (CETEM) and Geological Survey on separation methods, waste recovery, water use and material qualification, while Export Finance Australia and Brazil's BNDES could share due-diligence standards and help structure offtake agreements with Japanese, Korean, European or American buyers rather than subsidise each other's mines directly.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Names the specific institutions (ANSTO, CSIRO, CETEM, EFA, BNDES) that could operationalise a technical and financing partnership — a concrete institutional roadmap for investors or agencies tracking Australia-Brazil minerals cooperation.
insights.locator: Australia's ANSTO and CSIRO could work with

insights.claim: Both Australia's Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve and Brazil face the same financing problem: volatile prices can stop strategically useful mineral projects before they reach production, implying shared price-volatility risk management (not just technical cooperation) is a needed part of any bilateral compact.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Flags commodity price volatility as a shared, structural threat to critical-minerals project completion in both countries, relevant for assessing financing/hedging needs of new rare-earth and battery-metal projects.
insights.locator: Australia's reserve already recognises that volatile prices

insights.claim: The author explicitly states any Australia-Brazil minerals cooperation should not be sold as an anti-China arrangement, since China is Brazil's largest trading partner and Australia conducts a quarter of its trade with China; the aim is optionality — more processing locations, more qualified suppliers and more than one source of capital and demand — rather than exclusion of China.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Positions the proposed Australia-Brazil minerals partnership as diversification/optionality rather than a China-decoupling strategy — relevant framing for how such a partnership would likely be marketed to avoid alienating both countries' largest trading partner.
insights.quote: The practical aim is not exclusion. It is optionality: more processing locations, more qualified suppliers and more than one source of capital and demand.
insights.locator: None of this should be sold as an anti-China arrangement

insights.claim: Brazil would give Australia a large Latin American democracy with substantial resources, an industrial base and diplomatic reach across the Global South, while Australian mining-service firms would gain a deeper role in a market entering a major investment cycle, and Brazil would gain access to Australian regulatory experience, technology and project structures that could help it move beyond pure extraction.
insights.speaker: Gustavo Pessoa
insights.so_what: Lays out the reciprocal value proposition of a deeper Australia-Brazil minerals partnership, useful for Australian mining-services companies assessing Brazil as a growth market entering a major (US$77bn) investment cycle.
